solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Elitist-leaning set?

indicators.note: set read as a verb, as in a jelly set into a new shape, so the hyphenated phrase before it is rearranged

explanation.surface: A question about whether some group or clique has snobbish tendencies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set' looks like a noun meaning a group, which the whole clue also uses it as, but in the wordplay it says to rearrange the fourteen letters of ELITIST LEANING.
explanation.definitionFit: The intellectual elite of a society is a group often accused of snobbery, so the whole clue describes them.

clue.text: Beak's not available on half pay

definitions.note: a possessive noun standing for an adjective: belonging to the beak, i.e. the nose

indicators.note: half of a word means its first three of six letters are kept here

parts.note: pay as a noun is a salary

explanation.surface: A magistrate is told he cannot have his wages, since half-pay is off the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beak' is British slang for a magistrate as well as a nose; here it is the nose. 'half' keeps SAL from SALARY.
explanation.definitionFit: Beak is slang for the nose, and an adjective describing the nose is one relating to the nostrils, so 'of the beak'.

clue.text: Catch up with spouse but back off

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top, i.e. backwards
the back, or last letter, of the word is taken off

parts.note: a spouse is one's partner

explanation.surface: Someone catches up with their husband or wife, then retreats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back off' removes the final R of PARTNER to leave PARTNE, and 'up' turns that round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To trap someone is to snare or capture them, which is what catching them means.

clue.text: Noodle soup starter changing hands — food supplied is awful

indicators.note: the first letter swaps from right hand to left hand, R becoming L

parts.note: ramen is a Japanese noodle soup
a table is the food a host provides, as in 'keeps a good table'

explanation.surface: A recipe note: change the noodle soup starter and the resulting food is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L are the abbreviations for right and left, so 'changing hands' turns RAMEN into LAMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deplorable or very poor in quality is awful; both words describe grievously bad things.

clue.text: Dress game up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from the bottom, i.e. backwards

parts.note: brag is a card game, an ancestor of poker

explanation.surface: An instruction to make a game more dressy, or to dress up for a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Garb is clothing, an outfit; dress used as a noun means much the same attire.

clue.text: Little Greek character put in nick

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other, as a prisoner is put in a cell

parts.note: a nick is a small cut, a notch
mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A Greek man is locked up in a police cell, nick being British slang for prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nick' suggests the British slang for a prison, which suits 'put in', but here it is a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-word phrase meaning a small amount or hardly anything, the same as the noun little.

clue.text: Go on girl, put a drop of gin in it?

definitions.text: Go on girl, put a drop of gin in it?

indicators.note: the drop is placed inside the joined pieces, the it of the clue

parts.note: a go is an attempt, a shot
lass is a girl, especially in northern England and Scotland

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only the first letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: Someone urges a girl to add a splash of gin to her glass.
explanation.walkthrough: A semi-all-in-one: the whole clue paints the answer in use, while the wordplay puts just the first letter of gin into the other two pieces; 'on' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A small glass for a single measure of spirits is just the thing to pour a little gin into.

clue.text: A badly loaded trunk, short side first — it'll move as you walk

indicators.note: a trunk is loaded when something is packed inside it

parts.note: a trunk is a large storage box, a chest
ill can mean badly, as in 'ill-treated'
end-on means facing with the end, the narrowest side, foremost

explanation.surface: A trunk packed carelessly is carried narrow end forward, and will shift as you walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trunk' suggests luggage that would shift, but it is CHEST holding ILL; 'short side first' is END-ON, the short end facing forward.
explanation.definitionFit: The cord joining calf muscle to heel flexes with each step, so it is the body part that moves as you walk.

clue.text: Iran reacting to riots in strange land

indicators.note: to riot in something is to run wild in it, so these letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A news report of Iran's response to unrest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means unknown territory, a land not yet explored and so strange to the traveller.

clue.text: Old hands returned, mobbed by audience in island nation

indicators.note: something mobbed is surrounded by a crowd, so the other pieces go inside

parts.note: an ear is a hearing, an audience, as in 'give someone a fair ear'

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: mitts is slang for hands

explanation.surface: Veteran workers come back and are mobbed by a crowd in a far-off country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns the old hands round to STTIMO; 'audience' is a hearing, as in lending an ear, not a crowd of spectators.
explanation.definitionFit: Timor-Leste is an independent country occupying half of an island in the Malay Archipelago.

clue.text: Nipper excessively slight, lacking inches

parts.note: too means excessively, as in 'too hot'

indicators.note: lacking means without, so these letters are taken away

parts.note: slight means thin, slender
in is the abbreviation for inch or inches

explanation.surface: A child is far too skinny and falls short in height.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nipper' looks like a small child, which suits the surface, but here it is something that nips.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that nips or bites is a nipper, a playful word for one of the teeth.

clue.text: Study again about nonsense author's written for ending

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat; the 's is 'has'

indicators.note: the ending of the word written is its final letter

explanation.surface: A literary student revisits what a nonsense writer wrote by way of conclusion.
explanation.definitionFit: To go over material once more so as to master it again is to study it again.

clue.text: Good time girl of a type that may grow on one

definitions.text: of a type that may grow on one

parts.note: fun is a good time
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A party girl is the kind of person you might grow fond of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grow on one' sounds like growing to like someone; here it means mould or mushrooms growing on a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Moulds and athlete's foot are fungi, organisms that can grow on a body, so the adjective describes them.

clue.text: Animal feeding insects to mad hatter

indicators.note: feeding one thing to another puts it inside, as food goes in
mad means crazy, so the letters of the next word are scrambled

parts.note: bees are insects

explanation.surface: An animal is fed insects by the Mad Hatter, of Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland is a decoy: 'mad' scrambles the hatter into HARTET, which the insects go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a large African antelope with long curved horns, so it is a kind of animal.

clue.text: Ultra-cold Double Diamonds

parts.note: ice is slang for diamonds; Double says diamonds is used twice
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds, the second of the two

explanation.surface: Double Diamond was a pale ale heavily advertised in 1960s Britain, served very chilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double' says diamonds is clued twice: ICE (slang) then D (the card suit). The surface names Double Diamond, a British beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something chilled with frozen water is made very cold, so the adjective means extremely chilled.

clue.text: Language earns poet fans

indicators.note: to fan things is to spread them out, so these letters are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: A poet wins admirers through their way with language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fans' looks like a noun for admirers but is a verb meaning spreads out.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an artificial international tongue devised by Zamenhof in 1887, so it is a language.

clue.text: Soldier gets stressed when mentioned in dispatches — put it in a different way

definitions.text: put it in a different way

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper

indicators.note: mentioned here means spoken, so the word is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: frays means wears out or becomes stressed, as in 'tempers fray'

explanation.surface: A soldier under strain earns a commendation in military dispatches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mentioned in dispatches' is a British military commendation, but here it marks a sound-alike: FRAYS said out loud gives PHRASE.
explanation.definitionFit: To restate wording in other terms, expressing it differently, is to paraphrase it.

clue.text: Mafia bosses finding trade union slow to yield

parts.note: capi is the Italian plural of capo, a Mafia boss
late means slow or behind time, as of a clock

explanation.surface: Gangsters find that a labour union is slow to give in.
explanation.definitionFit: To capitulate is to surrender, give in to an opponent, which is what to yield means.

clue.text: React badly encountering lame, vacuous sentimentality

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so these letters are jumbled
vacuous means empty, so the middle of the word is emptied out, leaving its outside letters

explanation.surface: A critic reacts with disgust to weak, empty, mawkish writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' turns REACT into TREAC; 'vacuous' empties LAME to its outer letters LE.
explanation.definitionFit: Treacle is figuratively cloying sweetness, so it is used for mawkish, sugary sentiment.

clue.text: Don't tell anyone bishop's stashing bottles

indicators.note: to bottle something is to keep it contained, so the letters are inside these words

explanation.surface: A secret: the bishop has been hiding bottles of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottles' looks like a noun for the stash but is the verb containing the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a whispered sound used to attract attention discreetly, as when sharing a confidence.

clue.text: Gosh — unprincipled bird standing in for another

definitions.note: a phrase meaning a usurper put in place of someone else

indicators.note: a thing standing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: coo is a dated British exclamation of surprise, like gosh

indicators.note: unprincipled read as without its principal, i.e. first, letter

parts.note: a duck is a bird

explanation.surface: Exclaiming at a dishonest bird taking another's place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unprincipled' means losing the principal, or first, letter. The exclamation is old-fashioned British, like 'goodness'.
explanation.definitionFit: The bird lays its eggs in other birds' nests so its chick is raised in place of theirs, a usurper put in for another.

clue.text: Band involved in hold-up storing paintings in Germany

indicators.note: something storing another holds it inside

parts.note: art means paintings collectively

explanation.surface: A gang in a robbery hides stolen paintings in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band involved in hold-up' looks like a gang of robbers; it is an elastic band that holds up a stocking.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an elastic strap worn round the leg to keep a stocking or sock from slipping down.

clue.text: A drink and a biscuit

definitions.meaning: an American whiskey distilled mainly from corn
a British chocolate sandwich biscuit with a chocolate cream filling

explanation.definitionFit: The name covers both a Kentucky corn whiskey and a well-known British chocolate cream biscuit.

clue.text: Springiness not uniform in loaf

indicators.note: not says the following piece is absent from the word

parts.note: bounce is springiness or elasticity
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A baker notes that a loaf lacks consistent springiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loaf' suggests bread but is British slang for the head, as in 'use your loaf'; bonce is also British slang for head.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for the head; 'use your loaf' comes from rhyming slang loaf of bread.

clue.text: Clever bishop dividing beer

indicators.note: a piece dividing another splits it by sitting inside it

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A smart clergyman shares out the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone capable, skilful and talented is clever; both describe competence of mind.

clue.text: Classical verse with injection of humour finally would be funny

indicators.note: the answer, once it takes the injected letter, becomes the next word, so that letter is removed from that word

parts.note: ironic means wryly funny, paradoxical

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Old poetry spiced up with a touch of humour would make people laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse-style clue: inject R, the last letter of humour, into the answer and you get IRONIC, so the answer is IRONIC less that R.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionic metre is a classical Greek verse foot, two long and two short syllables, so the word names that verse form.

clue.text: Rob to achieve equal split after leaving wife

indicators.note: the wife leaves, so her letter is taken out of the phrase

parts.note: to break in two is to split into two equal parts

explanation.surface: After a wife walks out, a divorcing couple aims to divide everything equally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after leaving wife' removes W from BREAK IN TWO.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a house by force in order to steal is to rob it, so the phrasal verb means burgle.

clue.text: Veto bad nominee mistakenly named earlier

indicators.note: done mistakenly means in error, so these letters are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone blocks an unsuitable nominee who was wrongly put forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal term for something referred to previously in a document, named before.
